newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines reports major 1996 loss.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines reports major 1996 loss.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp. , which late last year narrowly averted financial failure through a controversial restructuring plan, reported on Wednesday the latest in a string of major annual losses.

Calgary-based Canadian, Canada's second largest carrier, warned investors in November that it would bleed more red ink in 1996 and embarked on a four-year strategy of route realignment and deep cost-cutting measures to stem the losses.

The survival plan took center stage nationally as the airline's management and unions and Canada's federal government locked horns over issues of employee wage cuts and Canada's airline deregulation policy.

Canadian, which has not posted a yearly profit this decade, said it suffered a 1996 net loss of C$187.1 million ($138.5 million), or C$4.23 ($3.13) a share, versus a 1995 loss of C$194.7 million ($144 million), or C$4.67 ($3.46) a share in 1995.
Operating revenues were C$3.1 billion ($2.3 billion), about flat with the previous year.
The fourth-quarter loss deepened to C$138.1 million ($102.2 million), or C$3.10 ($2.29) a share, from C$129.4 million ($95.8 million), or C$3.02 ($2.23) a share in the same period of 1995.
The company said widespread media coverage of its financial difficulties and high fuel costs weighed heavily on its 1996 results.
"In 1996 we recognized the need to improve our earnings in a substantial and immediate manner," Canadian's Chief Executive Kevin Benson said in a statement.

"To be successful our plans required the support of many different constituencies, creating a period of uncertainty in the last two months of the year. Unfortunately this resulted in a very poor performance for the fourth quarter of 1996."

The survival plan -- which still requires support from Canadian's 70 creditors -- includes C$60 million ($44 million) in expected annual savings by moving a quarter of its aircraft fleet to transborder routes from domestic flights.

A company-wide program to cut overhead costs was expected to save C$70 million ($52 million). The cost cuts included a C$48 million ($36 million) reduction in fees paid to AMR Corp. unit American Airlines, which owns a third of Canadian. The plan also includes C$70 million ($52 million) in
savings from employee wage cuts and fuel tax reductions from the governments of Canada, Alberta and British Columbia.
